title: Cyril and Methodius (9th century)
hookLine: brothers who made an alphabet so Slavs could pray in their own tongue
last: THE GARDEN OF THE MOTHER OF GOD.

lines: A PRINCE ASKS FOR A TEACHER.
cards: A message arrives in Constantinople from a Slavic prince far to the north. His people have heard Christian preachers, he says, but in languages they don't understand.
Send us a teacher who can explain the faith in our own words.
The emperor turns to two brothers from Thessalonica who grew up hearing Slavic spoken around them: one a scholar, the other an experienced administrator turned monk. There's one problem.
The Slavs have no letters, and you can't hand someone a Gospel in a language nobody has ever written down. Today, Cyril and Methodius.

teach.b: Our account is the old Slavonic life of the younger brother, who was called Constantine; he took the name Cyril only near the end, as a monk.
When the request came, the life says, Constantine prayed, and God showed him the letters.

teach.h: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.
teach.b: He made an alphabet and began to translate, and the first words he wrote were the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God."
The brothers went north and taught in the Slavic language. They translated the Gospels and the prayers of the liturgy, so people could hear the Mass in their own speech. Not everyone liked it.
Some clergy, the life says, argued that God could be praised only in three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Constantine answered with verse after verse of scripture.
One psalm, in the Douay-Rheims, says, "Let every spirit praise the Lord." Every spirit, not three languages.
The brothers traveled to the pope, who welcomed them and blessed their Slavonic books. Cyril died in Rome.
Methodius went back north as a bishop, and through hard years the work went on, after he was gone, in the hands of their students.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians both honor the two as saints, and John Paul the Second named them patrons of Europe, together with Benedict.
For the brothers, the Gospel was meant to reach people in the words they already spoke.

how: Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep a feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, and some Slavic churches, Catholic and Orthodox, still celebrate the liturgy in Church Slavonic, the language the brothers wrote down.

games.q: you're Constantine. a prince wants the Gospel in his people's language, but it has never been written. what do you do?
o: teach them Greek first, then the Gospel.
make letters for their language and translate.
send preachers who speak only Latin.
games.why: the life says he prayed, made an alphabet, and began with John: in the beginning was the Word.

practice: Think of someone near you whose first language isn't yours, a neighbor, a coworker, a grandparent, and a word they'd love to hear from you: hello, thank you, peace.

Breathe slowly and say it quietly a few times, getting the sounds right, standing for a moment inside another tongue. If you pray, thank God for the language you first prayed in, or first heard love in.
